title: Appearance
text: Reference

title: Appearance
text:
Settings → Interface → Appearance (Ctrl+,). Everything on that page belongs to Arbor rather than to Bennu, and changing it here
changes it in every Arbor window — the same page is in Corvus's settings, Merula's, the explorer's and Tyto's, and it is the same page, not a copy.

title: The pages under Interface
text:
Appearance

The theme, the chrome and the text size — below.

Animations

How fast transitions run, or whether they run at all.

Keyboard Inputs

The overlay drawing every key and chord you press, with the action each triggered — for demos, screencasts and pairing.

Terminals

The shells the built-in terminal offers. Bennu's terminal is Arbor's: the same shells, configured once.

title: The Appearance page
text:
Colour theme
The active theme, and the editor that makes new ones. The title bar's gear has the same list as a submenu, for switching without opening settings.
Window controls
A Mac-style trio on the left, or flat Windows controls on the right. Not shown on macOS, where the system paints the real ones.
Compact title bar
A shorter title bar, for a short screen.
Minimized dialogs cap
How many dialogs may sit parked in the status bar. Past it a minimize is refused with a toast; nothing parked is ever closed for you.
Font scale
Every piece of UI text together, from 80% to 140%. The editor's own font size is separate, under Editor.

title: Rearranging the rails
text:
Customize Activity Bar… — from the command palette, the title bar's gear, or the button on the Appearance page — decides what is on the two icon rails
and in what order: one tab per rail, and in each the top cluster (the tool windows) and the bottom one (the dock toggles).

• Drag the handle to reorder within a cluster.

• The eye hides a tool. It stays reachable — every one has a shortcut and a palette entry — it just stops taking a slot.

• Project carries a lock: it is the way in, and with no file open and no tree nothing on screen could open one.

• Restore defaults puts the current tab back in natural order with everything visible, without touching the other tab. Nothing is written until Save.

A Cargo root has no Structure, Maven or Forms button, so they are not there to arrange — but the arrangement you gave them on a Maven project is remembered, and comes back with them.

title: Where it is kept
text:
In the active profile's config.toml, beside the rest of the interface settings — never in the project. Two machines on one profile get the same bar; two
projects on one machine do not each get their own.

title: The welcome tour
text:
Bennu opens its first-run tour once, on the first launch. Welcome tour in the palette opens it again whenever you want, and it can be skipped from any step. It is
Bennu's own tour, with its own record of having been seen: going through Arbor's does not count, nor the reverse.

title: AssertJ
text: Build, run & test

title: AssertJ
text: The assertions that cannot fail — found in the test while you write it, rather than on the day the bug they were meant to catch reaches production with a green build.

title: The assertion that asserts nothing
text:
assertThat(x) builds an assertion object. Nothing is compared until a check such as isEqualTo is called on it, and the methods that only
configure it — as, describedAs, extracting, filteredOn, usingComparator — are not checks.

A statement that stops before a check is a warning: it compiles, runs and passes whatever the value is. The same goes for assertThatObject,
assertThatCode, the BDD then(…), and a soft-assertions object's softly.assertThat(…).
assertThatThrownBy(…) on its own is fine — it asserts that something was thrown.

title: Soft assertions nobody reports
text:
A SoftAssertions object does not throw: it collects, and throws everything at once when assertAll() is called. Forget that call and every failure
is collected into nothing.

The variable is flagged, and Alt+Enter on it offers Add softly.assertAll() as the method's last statement. The fix is offered only
where the end of the method is certainly the end of the test: no return in it, and no lambda or anonymous class using the variable.

The moment the variable goes anywhere — passed to a helper, returned, assigned — whoever receives it may call assertAll(), and nothing is said.
AutoCloseableSoftAssertions in a try-with-resources, SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(…) and the JUnit 5 extension report on their own and are never flagged.

title: Dedicated assertions
text:
A boolean assertion throws away the value it was computed from — the one thing you need when it fails in CI:

Written — Fails with — Alt+Enter rewrites to

assertThat(names.isEmpty()).isTrue() — expected true — assertThat(names).isEmpty()

assertThat(names.size()).isEqualTo(2) — expected 2 but was 3 — assertThat(names).hasSize(2)

assertThat(a.equals(b)).isTrue() — expected true — assertThat(a).isEqualTo(b)

assertThat(x == null).isFalse() — expected false — assertThat(x).isNotNull()

assertThat(x instanceof Order).isTrue() — expected true — assertThat(x).isInstanceOf(Order.class)

Also contains / doesNotContain, startsWith, endsWith, isPresent, and hasSize from a string's
length() or an array's length. The finding is a faint style note, and the rewrite is offered anywhere in the statement even when those notes are hidden.

The rewrites that depend on a type — isEmpty, hasSize, contains — are offered only when the variable's type is written
in the file as a JDK string, collection, map, Optional or array. On anything else there may be no such assertion, and the edit would not compile.

title: From JUnit to AssertJ
text:
With the caret in a JUnit 4 or JUnit 5 assertion, Alt+Enter offers Replace with AssertJ. In a file with two or more,
Replace every JUnit assertion in this file with AssertJ does them all in one edit.

JUnit — AssertJ

assertEquals / assertNotEquals — isEqualTo / isNotEqualTo

assertSame / assertNotSame — isSameAs / isNotSameAs

assertTrue / assertFalse — isTrue / isFalse

assertNull / assertNotNull — isNull / isNotNull

assertArrayEquals — containsExactly

The static import of AssertJ's assertThat is added with the edit when the file does not have it. The JUnit imports are left where they are.

A delta overload (assertEquals(1.0, ratio, 0.01)), a Supplier message (() -> "…"), a JUnit 4 assertTrue(label, flag)
whose first argument is not a literal, and assertArrayEquals over arrays whose types are not visibly the same. Nor in a file where a bare
assertThat already belongs to Hamcrest or a helper — the import would take the name away from it.

title: What it will not judge
text:
• Every call is resolved through the file's imports, never matched by name: Hamcrest's assertThat(x, is(1)), JUnit 4's, and a project's own helper are not
AssertJ's, and are left alone. A class implementing WithAssertions is recognised.

• assertThat(x instanceof T).isFalse() is not rewritten: isNotInstanceOf fails on null, where the original holds.

• A chain configured further than Bennu knows — usingRecursiveComparison().ignoringFields(…) with nothing after — is read as a check. That misses one, and
never reports a real assertion as broken.

• A test class extending JUnit 3's TestCase inherits its own assertEquals, so nothing in it is converted.

title: Assistant
text: Editor

title: Assistant
text:
A chat and agent panel on the right of the editor, opened with Alt+A or from the right rail.

Set it in Settings › Assistant. It is kept in a credential vault of its own and sent only to Anthropic,
with each request. Every message is billed to your key; the conversation shows what it has cost.

title: What is on the panel
text:
Part — What it does

Conversation — The title is a switcher: your conversations, today's first, each with the model it used, when it was last touched and what it cost. The pencil renames the open one, the … menu deletes it, and New conversation starts another. The open one shows as saved.

Context — How full the model's window is, as a bar split into instructions & tools, files & search results and the conversation. It stays calm until 75%, turns amber there and red past 90%, and offers Compact conversation…: it clears the output of older tool calls, then the model folds everything before your last message into a summary — and what you type in the dialog is what the summary must not lose, as with /compact "…" in Claude Code. A conversation that reaches 90% of the largest window you chose is compacted automatically (clearing first, summarising only if that is not enough), and the thread says so. Compacting costs one request, added to the conversation's cost. Open the line for the breakdown. Every figure is an estimate (about four characters to a token); the exact count comes back with each answer.

Thread — Your messages on the right; the assistant's as flowing text and highlighted code, with the tools it used folded into one line that opens on demand ("Read 2 files · Searched once"), and the changes it proposes as a card listing the files with their added and removed lines. The assistant answers in Markdown, rendered as headings, lists, tables, quotes, highlighted code and bold text, and the text is selectable. Hover an answer to copy it or to open it as a document — a Markdown editor (live preview, as in Bennu's .md tabs) where you can edit the answer, copy it or save it to a file; the conversation itself is not changed. Hover one of your own messages to copy it. Stop (the square where Send was) ends a run; what it had written stays.

Review — Opens the proposed changes as a diff, unified or side by side, with the files in a list on the left (↑ / ↓ move between them). In manual mode the window is where you decide: Apply all (Ctrl+Enter) or Reject all. A rejected card turns red and keeps its files readable; an applied one stays as a record and can be undone.

Model — Chosen at the composer, with what each is for, the size of its window and its price per million tokens (input / output). The list and the prices are a file, models.toml, built in; Settings › Assistant › Models and prices creates your own copy (assistant-models.toml in Bennu's config folder) where an entry with the same id replaces the built-in one and any other id is added — so a price change or a new model needs an edit and a Reload, not a new build. An entry gives [model.price] (input, output, and optionally cache_read, cache_write_5m, cache_write_1h) and, for a model that charges more for long prompts, [model.long_prompt] with over_tokens and its own rates. Cost is worked out request by request, with cache reads and writes at their own rates.

Context window — The largest window the assistant may use in this conversation: 50K up to 1M. A size the model cannot hold is listed but cannot be picked, and changing to a smaller model shrinks the window to fit.

Questions — Where it would otherwise guess, the assistant asks. Each question is a column of choices, one per row — pick one, or tick several — with Other… always there to type your own. When it asks several things at once, a strip of tabs names them (a tick once answered): jump to any, or use Back and Next, and the last step sends all the answers together, so changing an earlier one costs nothing. Answered, the card shrinks to what you decided and stays in the thread.

Reach — The shield beside Add context sets what it may touch: this file, this project (the default), all open projects, or anywhere on disk, which never asks. Reaching for anything outside the chosen scope raises one prompt that settles both questions: Deny, Allow reading or Allow reading & writing — for that folder, for the session. Secrets (.env, keys) and .git are never written. It may also be allowed to edit files and to use the Temp folders. Deleting is not a setting: every deletion asks.

Dry run — Turn it on from the … menu and Send shows the request instead of making it: the endpoint, the headers (the key masked, never shown), the JSON body exactly as it would go, and where its size comes from — instructions, tool definitions, conversation — with a rough cost. Show what would be sent… opens the same window at any time.

Composer — One quiet line under the text: the model, a settings menu and, in an agent conversation, the Auto switch. The settings menu holds the rest, each as a submenu showing its current value: Effort, Context window, Reach and Permissions. Chips above the text show what the message carries: the file you are in, the lines you selected, and the instruction files in play.

Agent · Chat — The switch in the header chooses between two kinds of conversation, kept apart. Agent works in the project through Bennu's tools. Chat has no tools on the project: it cannot read, search or change anything, and sees only what you type or select (its one tool is the help about Bennu itself) — for a question that has nothing to do with the project, or when you want to be sure nothing is touched. Each has its own list of conversations and its own home screen, and a conversation is one or the other for good; opening a chat from the list switches the panel to Chat.

Home — With no conversation open the panel shows its home: the mode you are in, the file and instruction files it would work with, a few things to begin with (an agent card sends a request at once; a chat card leaves the start of a sentence in the composer for you to finish) and your recent conversations. The panel opens on it.

Project instructions — The project's CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, and your own assistant-instructions.md in Bennu's config folder, are read into the assistant's instructions, so it follows the rules a team has already written down (the build command, conventions, what not to touch). Each file is cut at 16 KB and all together at 40 KB, and a file whose text repeats another is sent once. They appear as chips above the text; the instructions never override the access prompts or the ban on a shell. Turn it off in Settings › Assistant.

Git — Off by default; Settings › Assistant › Git turns it on. The assistant can then read the repository — status, diff, log and blame — and stage, unstage and commit, through Corvus's own git tools; it cannot push. Reading means commit messages and authors go to the provider, so Hide authors (on by default) shows the model each person as a made-up id such as Author-7f3a9c: the same person is always the same id, and the ids are turned back into names in what you read and in anything the assistant sends to git, so a commit message that credits an id credits the real person. A commit always asks first, even in Auto. Git is not available in a chat.

Plan — For work with several steps the assistant writes a plan first and ticks the steps off as it goes. The card in the thread lists them — done, in progress, still to do — with a bar and 3 of 7 · 43%. The percentage is steps done over steps planned: it says how much of the list is done, not how long the rest will take, and it goes down if the plan grows. It costs a little: the assistant writes the list again each time it changes, a few hundred tokens of output per update — in the order of a few cents for a task of several steps, a few percent of what such a task costs — and it is told to send updates alongside the tools it is already calling, so they add no requests of their own. Questions and small changes get no plan. Step plan in the composer's settings menu (and in Settings › Assistant) switches it off: the tool and its instruction are then not sent at all.

Spending limits — In Settings › Assistant › Spending limits, limits in euros: per conversation, per day (from midnight, your time), per week (from Monday) and per month. 0 switches one off; the defaults are €5 a conversation, €10 a day and €50 a month. A conversation or a period at its limit does not start another request, and a run in progress stops before the request that would take it over — the thread says which limit. The composer flags a limit from 80% (adjustable) and shows what the conversation has cost. Costs are recorded per run in a ledger of their own, so deleting a conversation does not hand its money back. Prices are in dollars, so amounts are converted at an exchange rate you keep by hand; with no usable rate a dollar counts as a euro.

Ask from the editor — A ✦ in the margin sits on the line the caret is on, or where a selection starts, and offers what fits what is there: Fix this error or Explain this problem when the editor has found a problem on the line; Explain, Look for bugs, Suggest improvements and Write tests for a selection; Explain, Write tests, Where is it used? and Write documentation for a declaration; and always Ask about this…, which leaves the start of a message in the composer. The request carries the file, the lines and the code itself, and starts a conversation of its own. Ask the assistant about this… in the Command Palette does the same from the keyboard, opening the menu at the caret. In a Markdown file, selecting a passage shows a small button at its end: Improve the writing, Make it shorter, Say more, Fix spelling and grammar, Translate. In the Run and Build output, the line that starts a stack trace has a Fix with the assistant button that sends the trace and asks for the cause in the project.

Help with Bennu — Ask how to do something in Bennu — a feature, a shortcut, where a panel is — and the assistant looks it up in Bennu's own documentation (and a map of the window's buttons and shortcuts) instead of answering from memory, which for a tool it has never seen would be invented. It works in a chat too. If the documentation has nothing, it says so.

Comments — In a Java or Rust file, a ✦ in the gutter sits on every doc comment — and, under the caret, on a declaration that has none. It opens: Improve this comment, Check against the code (parameters, return value, exceptions, statements the code contradicts), Make it shorter, Translate to English / Italian, or Write documentation. The request carries the file, the lines and the declaration, so there is nothing to type; the result comes back as a proposal like any other edit.

Settings — The … menu opens Settings › Assistant: the API key (kept in a credential vault of its own, apart from the one holding your git tokens, and never in a config file), the model, window and mode a new conversation starts with, and the same reach choices plus the extra folders it may work in.

Manual · Auto — Manual: you approve every edit — reject, review the diff, or apply. Auto: edits are applied as they are proposed, each one can be undone, and the card stays as a record.

title: How it is meant to work
text:
• It reads and edits the project only through Bennu's own tools — files, search, usages, beans, endpoints, diagnostics, and the refactoring engine (rename, add parameter, change case) — never a shell. rename_symbol and add_parameter work from the project index and change every file they touch as one change — proposed for you to review in Manual mode, applied in Auto — and a renamed public type's file is renamed with it.

• Several changes at once. edit_files makes a list of exact edits across files as one change — all or nothing, one request — and replace_in_files replaces text or a regular expression across a folder (with a dry run first, and a limit on how many files it will touch). structural_replace rewrites code by its shape using Bennu's structural search, which is safer than a regular expression. All of them arrive as a proposal in Manual mode and are applied, and recorded in Local History, in Auto.

• Local History. It can list a file's revisions, show what changed, list deleted files and restore one — a restore is an edit like any other, proposed or applied by your mode.

• Showing you things. Ask to see the vulnerabilities, the problems, the module graph or Find in Files and it opens that window instead of describing it.

• Tool families. Settings › Assistant › Tools it may use switches off groups of tools — reading and search, project intelligence, editing, refactoring, structural replace, Local History, build and run. A group that is off is not offered at all.

• Several projects. With the reach set to All open projects the assistant works across the projects open in the workspace — the one you are in first, up to the number set in Settings › Assistant › Projects at once (6 by default). It reads, searches and changes in all of them: each is named in its instructions, a tool takes a project by name (or name:path), the text search and the file finder take project: "all", and a change goes to the project that owns the file, which keeps its own Local History. A proposal names a file in another project as name:path.

• Ctrl+Enter sends; Enter is a new line.

• The file you are in and the lines you have selected travel with the message, shown as chips above the text; the selection is read when you click into the composer.

title: Bean Validation
text: Java & JSP

title: Bean Validation
text:
A constraint's message is resolved against a bundle the validator chooses — almost never the bundle the rest of the application reads, and sometimes
named in a @Bean. Bennu finds it, and checks the keys against it.

title: The assumption that is wrong
text:
")
private String name;`, 'java')}

The application has messages.properties, the field has that message, and it is entirely natural to assume the two go together. They do not.

Bean Validation resolves a message key against ValidationMessages — that exact base name, at the classpath root — plus the provider's own
bundle inside its jar, where the defaults of @NotNull and friends live.

A key that exists in messages_it.properties and nowhere else is one the validator cannot find, and it renders the key itself — braces included — into the field
the user is looking at.

That is why constraint messages are checked apart from the other message bundles. The bundle tooling answers does any bundle declare this key — true, and the wrong
question. Here the question is whether the validator can find it.

title: Where the bundle is named
text:
The specification's

ValidationMessages.properties

On a resource root, in every locale written. Nothing declares it — being called that is the declaration, which is also why it wears an icon of its own in the project tree, locale variants included: it is the one .properties among dozens that decides what a person filling in a form reads.

Named in code

A resource bundle locator

A base name in a string literal in a method body — in no configuration file, nothing to grep for — redirecting every custom message. An AggregateResourceBundleLocator naming several is read the same way.

Spring's

setValidationMessageSource(…)

Points the validator at the application's own MessageSource — the one wiring that makes the natural assumption true. Recorded as such, and checked against those bundles.

`, 'java')}

A bundle the code names and no file provides is flagged on the line naming it, rather than on the hundred messages it breaks: every custom message resolved through it
renders as its own key, all at once, and nothing else in the project looks wrong.

title: What counts as a key
text:
A message is interpolated, and only one of the things that can appear in it is a bundle key:

Written — Is

{min} on a @Size — The constraint's own attribute, resolved before any bundle

{order.name.length} — A bundle key

${validatedValue} — An expression, evaluated at interpolation — never looked up

\{ — An escaped brace, printed as written

Not cosmetic: reading every brace as a key would report min and max missing on every custom @Size message. Bennu knows each
constraint's attributes, so it reports the one genuinely unresolvable. Keys in the provider's own bundle —
jakarta.validation.constraints.NotNull.message, and its javax spelling — are resolvable though nothing in your project declares them: they are in the jar.

title: In the editor
text:
Completion
Inside a message's braces, the keys the validator can resolve, with their text — deliberately not every key in the project: offering one from messages.properties would teach the mistake.
Hover
On a key, what the message will say and which bundle it comes from; on the annotation, what the constraint checks and which attributes its message may interpolate.
Go to declaration
On a key, the bundle line defining it, one target per locale.

An error

No validator for the type

@NotBlank on an int, @Size on a long: Hibernate Validator refuses it at startup — not a wrong message, an application that does not come up.

A warning

A constraint that can never fail

@NotNull on a primitive reads as a rule and enforces nothing.

A project type, a type variable, or a JDK class beyond those Bean Validation names produce no diagnostic: a custom ConstraintValidator is invisible from here,
and Bennu will not contradict one it cannot see. On a project with no validation bundle nothing is said about keys at all — the messages are literals or defaults.

title: The Constraints panel
text:
Every constraint the project declares, in one list: the member it is on, the message it will show, and its type as a tag. Group by constraint to answer "where do we use
@Email".

The tag to look for is missing: — a row whose message names a key no validation bundle declares. On screen, a constraint whose message does not resolve
looks exactly like one whose message does, until a user trips it.

title: Bevy ECS
text: Rust

title: Bevy ECS
text:
In an ECS the architecture is the data: a component and the systems that read and write it say more about how a game works than any file layout. Bennu reads
that out of the source — the declarations, the system signatures, and the pairs of systems whose accesses cannot run at the same time. No build, no running game.

title: When it turns on
text:
On a project whose Cargo manifest declares bevy or any bevy_* crate, corroborated by the sources — a #[derive(Component)], an
add_systems call. Which signal convinced Bennu is listed under Projects. A Maven project never carries this tooling.

title: Components
text:
Alt+Shift+B, or the rail button. One row per declared Component, Resource, Message,
Event, Bundle and States, badged. Expand a row for the systems touching it — each naming the system, whether it reads or writes,
and the parameter it was read from:

{`Health Component read by 2 · written by 1
damage write mut q: Query Update
draw_health read q: Query> Update
PlayerBundle in bundle carries Health`}

This is find usages asked properly: who writes Health is a question about signatures, and a text search answers it with every comment mentioning the word.

A marker
A component nothing reads, whose whole job is With<Player>, is counted apart, as filtered on by. A filter is not an access — two systems filtering on one marker do not contend — but a marker twenty queries depend on is not unused either.
Messages and events
Two roles, not two names: a message is buffered — written with a MessageWriter, drained by whoever reads it — an event is triggered and delivered to observers. A message is found through the queue it is posted to, an observer event through the On<…> parameter handling it.

title: Systems
text:
One row per system, badged by the schedule it was registered in, so grouping by badge groups by schedule. The row summarises what it touches; expanding lists each access
with its query filters. A system with no add_systems call found is tagged so rather than hidden — on a project registering through a helper, that tag is the
honest answer.

title: Access conflicts
text:
Two systems in one schedule wanting the same data, one of them mutably, can never run in parallel. Bevy derives that from the signatures when it builds the schedule, and so
does this panel:

{`damage ⇄ tick Update contend over Score unordered
Score write/write — mut score: ResMut
tick mut score: ResMut`}

Working as intended

ordered

Two conflicting systems explicitly ordered — what .before, .after and .chain are for.

Worth a look

unordered

Serialised in whichever order the schedule picks: a frame-order dependency nobody wrote down.

An exclusive system — one taking &mut World — contends with everything in its schedule, and gets one row saying so rather than one per component.

Only an unordered pair is also mentioned in the editor, as a single informational note on the name of each system that lists its peers (contends with 3 unordered
systems (a, b, c) over Score). Contention without a declared order is the normal state of most Bevy projects, so it is never a warning. Ordering is followed transitively —
a.before(b) plus b.before(c) orders a against c — and .after and .chain() count the same way.
The note is left out when Bennu cannot stand behind it: a system in a set (a set's ordering is declared by configure_sets, which Bennu does not
read), an exclusive one, a system registered with a .run_if(…), and a pair that only meets through a message buffer, one side writing and the other
reading. All of them still appear in the panel.

title: In the editor
text:
Mark — Beside

◈ — A component

▣ — A resource

✉ — A message

✳ — An observer event

▦ — A bundle

Clicking one opens the systems that touch it — one jumps, several ask.

title: Engines built on Bevy
text:
A project on an engine of its own may never write Res or MessageReader: it declares #[derive(DomainResource)] and takes a
DomainResMutParam<Board>, and the engine's parameter does the Res underneath. Bennu reads the wrapper as what it wraps, so the declaration still
lists its systems and a contending pair still pairs.

The wrappers known are fulcrum's per-domain layer — DomainResParam, DomainResMutParam, DomainStateParam,
DomainStateMutParam, DomainMessageReader, DomainMessageWriter, DomainQuery — and its derives DomainResource,
DomainMessage, DomainState. A #[derive(SystemParam)] the project itself declares is read from its own fields and needs no table.

title: Where a component is created
text:
A signature says who reads a component; nothing in one says who makes it — so a type six systems read has, by its parameters alone, no origin. Under
every declaration is a row per site putting it into the world: a spawn, an insert on an existing entity, an insert_resource, an
add_message, an init_state — each naming its function and the argument given.

Read from call sites, so spawn((Health(100.0), Player)) is a row under Health and one under Player — what a bundle-as-tuple means. A value
whose type cannot be named from the expression is skipped, and the call names are a closed list: an insert method on your own type contributes nothing.

title: Materials and shaders
text:
A #[derive(Asset)] type is a row in the components list like any other — "who touches SpiralHoverMaterial" is answered by the same signatures. An asset
is reached through the Assets<T> resource storing it, which is how it is looked up here. A material carries its shaders as the first rows under it, and the
relationship is described in Shaders (WGSL).

title: What it does not claim
text:
Bennu reads this project's own sources and nothing else — not the engine's plugins, not a dependency's systems — which decides what is safe to say:

A conflict stays true
Two systems contending over Score contend however many systems a plugin adds — so the report is short of pairs rather than full of invented ones.
Disjoint queries are not conflicts

With and Without on the same component keep two queries apart, and so does a plain &T / &mut T / Mut<T> /
Ref<T> in the query data, which requires T just as With<T> does — Query<(&mut A, &mut B)> never overlaps
Query<&mut B, Without<A>>. An Or<…> filter makes no claim at all.

Run conditions and tests are not read as a schedule
Whether a .run_if(…) is true cannot be known from the source, so a conditional system is never accused. Code under #[cfg(test)], #[test] functions and mod tests is skipped, so an App built inside a test does not invent pairs.
Parallelism is never claimed
"These two run at the same time" cannot be shown from part of a schedule: one unseen system writing the same component would refute it.
No ordering graph
Most of an app's ordering lives in plugins, so a picture from this project's add_systems calls would be a fragment presented as a whole. Ordering appears only as the tag on a conflict row. Systems are matched to the open file by name and position, so a same-named function in another module, or a method called like a system, does not collect another system's note.
Names are not resolved
Health is matched by name, so two Health types in two modules look like one — though generic arguments are kept, so NextState<GameState> and NextState<MenuPage> stay apart. Every row shows its parameter, so a wrong one can be recognised.
Registration is read literally
A system added behind a cfg, in a loop or by a macro is not seen as registered — it appears with no schedule.

title: Rust & Cargo
text: Rust

title: Rust & Cargo
text:
What a Cargo workspace is, what you can run on it, and what is wrong with its manifests — all of it read from the files rather than asked of
cargo.

title: The Cargo tool window
text:
Alt+8 opens it on a Rust project. Its rail button is there whenever the workspace has a Cargo project — at a project's root
or in a subfolder, as in a Tauri app — and sits beside Maven's when it also has a Java one.

title: Several Cargo projects
text:
The window lists the Cargo projects of the whole workspace, not only the project on screen: a Rust crate in a
subfolder of a Node project (a Tauri app's src-tauri) is a Cargo project like any other, and so is one in
another project of the workspace. With more than one, a small tree at the top — grouped by project when the workspace has
several — picks the one the commands act on. Pick a row with Enter or a click; pick it again to let go. With
nothing picked the window follows the file you are editing; with a single Cargo project there is no tree at all.

The same rule applies to the palette: a command that acts on one Cargo project runs straight away when a row is picked or the
open file belongs to one, and otherwise asks which, in a list you can filter by typing.

The first group is the whole workspace — every command aimed at every crate, --workspace. Under it, one group per crate,
each holding three things:

Click to run, with -p

Commands

check, build, test, run, clippy, fmt, doc — output in the Run console.

Discovered, not only read

Targets

The binaries, examples, integration tests, benchmarks and the library. src/main.rs and src/bin/*.rs are Cargo's conventions, not the manifest's, and each row says which it was. A binary or example runs when clicked; anything else opens its source.

What the crate declares

Features

The ones default reaches, transitively, are marked, with what each turns on. An optional dependency's implicit feature is listed — unless something refers to it as dep:…, Cargo's own rule for suppressing it.

The crate header answers what the three groups cannot — where the crate is. Its locate button, or Focus in
Project from a right-click on the header, opens the Project tree on the crate's folder, expanded, selected and holding the keyboard focus. The
same menu opens its Cargo.toml and copies its path.

The common commands are in the command palette too — "Cargo: …", aimed at the whole workspace — since a row can only be clicked with the
panel open.

title: Two things it tells you unprompted
text:
A directory under the root with a Cargo.toml no members pattern covers. Otherwise silent: it compiles when built directly and is
invisible to --workspace. The panel names it and offers to open the manifest missing it. A crate inside another crate's tree is not flagged —
that is how a fixture crate is written.

cargo clippy without the component fails with an unknown-subcommand error, which reads as a broken button. The row says needs clippy
instead, and rustup component add clippy then ⟳ fixes it. Without rustup at all nothing is greyed: not knowing is not knowing it
is absent.

title: Cargo.toml
text:
A manifest gets completion and diagnostics of its own, both from one description of what a manifest may contain — which is why a key that completes can
never underline itself as unknown.

Completion:

Ctrl+Shift+Space, or just type. What is offered depends on the caret:

The caret — Offered

In a [header] — The tables, minus those already there — except [[bin]] and friends, where a second is the point

On a key — The table's keys not yet set, each with a line saying what it does

After a dot — workspace, on the keys Cargo lets a member inherit — nothing on name, which it does not

In a dependency table — Crate names from this workspace, Cargo.lock and the crates already downloaded; accepting writes the whole assignment with the newest known version

On a version — The versions this machine has, newest first — a pre-release never above its release

Inside a spec — version, path, git, features, optional, workspace, …

A value with a closed set — Editions, crate types, lint levels — with quotes when the caret is not in a string

In [features] — The other features, the optional dependencies, and both reference forms, dep:serde and serde/

In members — The directories holding a crate, and the dir/* glob covering what is under one

The crate list is what this machine has seen, so the popup appears while you type. What crates.io answers is the two questions below, off the same cached index.

Newer versions:

A dependency that is behind gets a line above it — 1.0.219 available — and pressing it writes that version into the manifest as one undo step. It is
deliberately quiet:

• nothing about a path, git or workspace-inherited dependency, which has no version to be behind;

• nothing about a pin (=1.2.3) or a range — you already decided;

• nothing about a pre-release, either way.

Answers come from an on-disk cache refreshed at most daily per crate, and a failed lookup falls back to whatever was cached — offline, last week's list beats
silence. Settings → Rust turns it off, making Bennu entirely local again.

title: Adding a dependency
text:
• Press the ＋ in the Cargo window's toolbar, or Add dependency… in the palette.

• Type the crate name, then pick a published version and the features that version declares.

• Pick the table — dependencies, dev-, build- — and, in a workspace, the member.

It runs the real cargo add: the requirement written cargo's way, [workspace.dependencies] inheritance honoured, the features validated
against the resolved crate, the entry in the file's own style. When cargo refuses, its words are shown — they are the fix. Afterwards the manifest is read again,
the crate graph refreshed and the language server told to resolve the project.

The index Cargo uses has no search: a crate is looked up by name. An unknown name or an unreachable index still adds — leave the version empty and cargo picks it.

Diagnostics:

Silent in Cargo

A key typo

[dependancies], feature = […] — the symptom is a dependency that is not there or a feature that does nothing, in a manifest that looks fine.

Refused by Cargo

A feature referring to nothing

Usually after a rename. All four reference forms are understood, and a bare name that is a non-optional dependency gets its own wording — the fix is optional = true.

Plus:

• workspace = true with no matching entry in the root's [workspace.dependencies] or [workspace.package];

• a path or members entry with no crate behind it; a default-members entry that is not a member;

• a duplicate key; a dependency naming both a git and a path, or no source at all;

• an optional dev-dependency; a version requirement with no number in it.

Red is only for what Cargo refuses to build. An unknown key is a warning — Cargo warns on those and gains new ones every few releases. Nothing is said about a table
Bennu does not recognise, or anything under [package.metadata] and [lints.*], which belong to other tools.

title: Dependencies
text:
Alt+N opens the panel a Maven project uses, in Cargo's vocabulary: one group per crate, and per row the crate, the version,
where that version came from, its kind — normal, dev, build — and whether it is in the local registry.

• The version is the one Cargo.lock chose, not the requirement written — serde = "1" is not what you compile against. With no lockfile
the panel says so and shows the requirement, unknown rather than missing.

• A workspace = true dependency is marked as pinned by the workspace; a renamed one shows both names; a target-specific one carries its
cfg(…).

• The last group is everything in the lockfile no crate of yours declares — what your dependencies dragged in.

title: Running and debugging
text:
▶ and Shift+F10 launch the active run configuration, and a Cargo configuration is a cargo subcommand: a crate, a command, a
target, features, a profile, and two argument fields. On a workspace with exactly one binary none of it is needed — ▶ makes the configuration and runs it. With several
it opens the editor, because cargo run refuses to guess too.

Field — Goes — Reaches

Cargo arguments — Before the -- — cargo

Program arguments — After it — Your program or the test harness — --nocapture belongs here

A cargo run has no build step in front of it — the command is the build. Its output, Stop, ⟳ and the tab strip are the Run console's usual ones. Debugging a
Cargo configuration builds the binary first and launches it under a debug adapter — see Debugging.

title: Navigating
text:
Ctrl+N opens the navigator on Types rather than Classes — structs, enums, traits and type aliases — and
Ctrl+Shift+Y finds functions, methods and constants. The language server does the matching, so both start at two characters.

Both of its views read Bennu's own engines — tree-sitter grammars for Java and JSP, and Java's declaration model — so on a Rust project it could only report their
absence, which would read as Bennu not understanding a language rust-analyzer is answering everything about. The rail slot holds the Cargo window instead.

title: Generated Rust
text:
Settings → Rust → Code Style says how a code template writes Rust — read as style.rust
in a template. It is a short list, and deliberately: rustfmt owns the formatting, and a second set of
switches here would either agree with the project's own rustfmt.toml or fight it. What is left is what a
generator has to decide and a formatter never touches:

• Visibilitypub, pub(crate) or private, for a generated item and its fields

• Deriveswhat a generated struct or enum derives, in order — empty writes no #[derive(…)] line

• Documentation linesa /// on each generated item, which is what missing_docs asks for on anything public

• Errorsanyhow::Result, a crate error type, or a Result<T, E> spelled out

• Self inside implSelf rather than the type's name — Clippy's use_self

The page carries a preview of a small generated type, so each choice is read in the output rather than in its label.
Java's equivalent is Settings → Java → Code Style, and the two are separate because almost nothing
they say overlaps.

title: Completion
text: Editor

title: Completion
text: What the popup knows, where each suggestion comes from, and the members that exist without being written anywhere.

title: Asking for it
text:
Typing . after an expression offers the members. Ctrl+Space — or Ctrl+Shift+Space — asks explicitly, anywhere. In Java the answers come from the project index and appear once it is warm; edits are indexed
again in the background as you type, so completion and go-to follow your changes without reopening anything.

Not a style choice. macOS claims the whole Ctrl+Space family for switching input source, above
applications: those chords produce no key event in any program. Cmd+Space is Spotlight, which is what the
Shift is for.

• Typing fast does not send a question per key. Within a burst the list is asked for when you pause, and at least every few hundred
milliseconds while the burst lasts; the first letter, a . and Ctrl+Space are answered at once.

• When an explicit request finds nothing, the footer says so for a moment — No suggestions here, or No engine answered for
this file when no server or index is up. Silence would look like a shortcut that never arrived, and those two have opposite fixes.

• If a shortcut seems to do nothing at all, turn on Show keyboard inputs (Alt+Shift+K) and press it again: the overlay draws every chord the window receives. Nothing drawn means the key never arrived — a
conflict outside Bennu.

• Command languages ask on every position. A .dev scenario or a .dig line is words and
arguments rather than dotted paths, so with the caret after unlock the server — nd-dig-lsp, geode's
own — is asked too, not only after a trigger character.

title: The order things are offered in
text:
What comes first is worked out from what the engine already knows, and it decides most of what completion feels like. Strongest first:

• What the position wants. The only term about the hole rather than the candidate. In
String name = order. there are forty members on order and a handful that can be written there — and nothing
about order says which, because the constraint is left of the =. It is read from a declaration with a written
type, an assignment to something typed, a return — a lambda's too — and a condition, which wants a boolean and
turns a member list into its predicates. The exact type comes before a subtype, and the only exact match is preselected: return Ra
in a method returning RawIdentity opens on RawIdentity, return builder. on build(), a bare
return on the local or field of that type. With a generic return, Optional<RawIdentity>, the element type follows
the outer one. A void method sinks where a value is wanted. It ranks, never filters: hiding the misses would hide the
right answer whenever the type is not the one expected.

• Who declares it. After a dot, what the receiver's own type declares comes first, then what it inherits — the nearest
supertype first — then java.lang.Object's, last. A record's components come before the equals,
hashCode and toString the compiler writes for it. Only the position's type and how literally your letters match
come before this: route. opens on prefix(), preselected, while route.to still offers
toString above a declared targetOrigin.

• What you picked last time. A fact about you, not the code: on a List you reach for stream,
not listIterator. Kept per declaring type, so what is learned about java.util.List carries to every
receiver inheriting it. Frequency and recency both count, so a fresh choice can overtake an old habit and one stray pick cannot bury a
name you use constantly. It lives for the session and is never written to disk — a persisted ranking that drifted would be invisible.

• What the receiver is. After a type — Color. — the statics are the answer and a constant goes to
the very top, instance members to the bottom. Through a value — color. — the other way round, more gently: a
static through an instance compiles, it is just rarely meant.

• Deprecated. Still offered, since you may be reading old code, but last — on your own source, since library members
carry no annotations in compiled form.

• What this file already uses. A name already in the buffer is likely wanted again. It decides between otherwise-equal
candidates, and cannot do more.

• The name being filled. String customerName = c. has three String members and the alphabet puts
email first; the declaration says name. A candidate whose words echo the hole's rise — getName reads as
name, orders as order, a shared tail or head counts less than the whole name. In an argument slot the
hole is named by the callee: findByCustomerId( lifts customerId.

• What the project does. How often the project calls each method, and which method it calls after the previous one in
the chain — close() after open(), on the same variable even when the calls are statements apart. Counted while
the index builds, as a band (each step a doubling, a name used once counts for nothing), never written to disk.

The last two, and the shape of the code below, are Smart suggestions in Settings → Completion: each is a switch, and a
strength scales the learned ones. They only add to a score — nothing is hidden — and none can overrule the type the position wants.

title: Smart suggestions
text:
Chains
When the position wants a type, members of members that produce it are offered below the direct fits: String name = order. also
lists getCustomer().getName(). Zero-argument calls only, one level deep, through your own classes; a member that already
fits is not chained through, and a call that is already written gets none.
Builders
A setter already called in the chain sinks: after Order.builder().customer(c). the next property or build() leads, not
customer again.
Unused locals
A local declared and not used yet rises: it is very probably what comes next.
catch (
The exceptions the try above can throw come first — from throw new and from the throws clause of each call it
makes (the first few calls; one that cannot be bound to a single overload says nothing). A multi-catch leaves out the alternatives it
already lists, and a second catch reads the same try.

Keywords come below anything the index resolved. Words scraped from the buffer are offered only when the index answered nothing —
before it finished building, or in a file no project owns: they are a regular expression over the text, and beside resolved names they bury
them under look-alikes. How well what you typed matches still decides between neighbours.

Type names:

A simple name usually resolves to several types, so type names get two terms of their own:

What this file has said
Nothing outranks it: a type the file imports, then a package it wildcard-imports, then its own package, which needs no import.
What the project imports
Every import in the codebase is somebody choosing a candidate, and the aggregate predicts the next choice. It is weighed against distance — the nearest package by shared prefix, so a sibling beats a cousin — with the JDK ahead of the rest of the classpath, because a name matching both a JDK type and something in a jar you never opened is almost always the JDK one.

The two are weighed, not ordered, and the balance is the point: java.util.List imported in four hundred files beats an
it.acme.model.List nobody imports, though the second is nearer. A type imported once beats nothing — that is a
coincidence, not evidence.

Settings → Completion → Order type names by what this project imports switches the second term off at once. What the file
itself imports still comes first — that was never a statistic.

title: Where the import counts come from
text:
They are counted while the index builds, in the pass that already parses every file — one lookup per import
line. Nothing is written to disk: a saved copy would go stale, and a project that dropped a library would go on recommending it with nothing
saying why. They are not updated as you type either — whether a codebase uses java.util.List does not change because you saved
a file, and an order shifting under you would be worse than one a rebuild behind. They refresh with the index.

A count is used as a band: each step a doubling, stopping at 128. Four imports against eight is real; four hundred against
eight hundred is not, and a ranking that pretended otherwise would pin one ubiquitous type to the top for ever. A wildcard counts for the whole
package, one band weaker.

title: How a name is matched
text:
A name does not have to be spelled the way it is declared. What you type is matched three ways, best first, and which one
matched is part of the order:

Match — Typed — Reaches

An exact prefix — toLo — toLowerCase

A prefix ignoring case — TOLO — toLowerCase — a shift held one letter too long

The camel humps — tolc, aAE, SBA, MAXV — toLowerCase, addAllElements, SpringBootApplication, MAX_VALUE — an underscore starts a word too

It is one rule for every kind of candidate — a member, a local, a static import, a class name.

Settings → Completion → Popup decides when the popup arrives and how forgiving it is: whether it opens on its own while you
type, after how long a pause, or only on the chord; and case-sensitive matching. That last is about case, not humps — off, only the
first letter must agree, the one that carries information in Java since a capital means a type; on, every letter must, so aAE
still reaches addAllElements and aae no longer does.

title: A name with nothing to its left
text:
Java says exactly what a bare identifier can mean, and the popup offers those things nearest first:

• What the scope binds — locals, method and lambda parameters, the for variable, a try-with-resources, a
catch parameter, a pattern variable from o instanceof Foo f. A variable of this block beats a parameter of the
method; in one block, the line above beats twenty lines up. A shadowing name is offered once, as the inner one — what the name resolves to.

• The enclosing type's own members, and what it inherits, without this..

• What an import static brought in, with the type it came from on the row — the one case where nothing else
on screen says where a bare name is from.

• Class names, from the type-name index.

A local is not in scope inside its own declaration, so int counted = coun offers counter, not counted.
In a static method an instance member is not offered at all: it would not compile.

Str is a type being written and str a variable, and no score makes one the other. A capitalised name with a
lowercase letter leads with types; anything else leads with what is in scope, where a SCREAMING_CASE constant of your own class
lives. Both lists are always offered, so a prefix read the "wrong" way costs a scroll, not an answer.

title: What accepting one writes
text:
A method is a call: accepting size writes size(). When it takes arguments the caret lands between the
parentheses, where the parameter hints strip is about to describe them; when it takes none, after them.

• Parameter names are not written — tabbing through put(key, value) placeholders to delete them is slower than typing,
and a class file carries no names anyway.

• When the call is already written — t.si() with the caret after si, correcting a name — the
parentheses are left alone, not doubled.

• An overloaded method is one row per overload, fewest parameters first — wait(),
wait(long timeoutMillis), wait(long timeoutMillis, int nanos) — since each leaves the caret in a different place.
After :: they are one row, because a method reference writes only the name. A method that merely overrides an
inherited one appears once.

• What could not be written there is not offered: a private member of another class, a package-private one from another package,
and a protected one through a receiver outside its package and your class — route.clone() and
route.finalize() are not Java, this.clone() is.

title: Reading a row
text:
The icon
What it is. A member is a circle — m method, c constructor, f field,
v variable, p parameter — and a type a rounded square — c class, i interface,
e enum, r record, @ annotation; a package is a folder, a template {'{}'}. A dot in the
corner marks static, a lock final, a dashed outline abstract, a diagonal stroke deprecated.
The name
What it is called, with the letters you typed marked. Bold when the receiver's own type declares it,
regular when inherited, dimmed when it is java.lang.Object's. A deprecated one is struck through.
The parameters
Beside the name, with their names where the member carries them: equals(Object obj). A library compiled without
parameter names shows the types alone.
The right edge
What a method returns or a field holds — getClass() as Class<? extends ServiceRoute>,
typed after the receiver — and, for an inherited member only, where it comes from: what tells List.of from
Set.of.

The documentation of the highlighted row appears beside the list — the card hover draws, from the same answer, so the two
cannot describe one member two ways. It is fetched only for the row you highlight: a library's documentation is read from its sources archive,
and doing it for four hundred rows would put an archive read per candidate on the keystroke that opened the popup.

title: Type names and their imports
text:
Typing a capitalised name (not after a dot) offers every class matching it across the JDK, your dependencies and your
project, each with its package — and (+N more) when several packages declare the name. Within each match tier your project's types
come before a jar's, and shorter names before longer.

• Accepting a name that maps to a single class adds its import — turn that off with Settings → Completion →
Auto-import on accept. An ambiguous name inserts just the name; Alt+Enter → Import '…'
picks the package.

• A qualified name completes one segment at a time: import org. offers springframework, and
import org.springframework.boot. offers its packages beside its classes.

• A receiver not imported yet still completes: Arrays. without the import offers its members, and accepting
one adds the import too — for an unambiguous name only.

• A type receiver offers its nested types beside the statics — Map. offers Entry.

A nested type completed by its simple name is written through its outer, since Inner alone is not a name Java resolves:

One import serves every nested type of that class, the form people write by hand. Where the simple name is already in scope nothing is added:
inside the outer class or a sibling nested in it, and in a file that imports the nested type outright.

Other languages:

In TypeScript and JavaScript — and in a .svelte file and an Angular project's templates — the popup
is the language server's: typescript-language-server, svelteserver, ngserver. Install it from Settings →
Language Servers; without one the file is still coloured, folded and edited, with nothing to suggest.

No language server will serve a JSP — a template that prints JavaScript, half of it <%= %> holes. The names the block
declares (var, function, foo: function (…) and their parameters) come first, then the browser globals.
After document., location., Math. and the rest of the platform, the members are read off the object
itself in the engine the page runs in — not a list that could be stale. Hover says the same. What it cannot know is jQuery:
$ is offered, $(…). has no object to read.

title: Annotations
text:
Typing @ opens the popup on its own, with annotation types only — from every type on the classpath to
the few hundred annotations on it, so the list is short and nearly always holds the answer.

• It narrows again from where the caret is: above a field, one whose @Target only allows a method sorts below the ones that belong
there. Ranked, not hidden — an annotation from unread bytes reports no target, and reading that as a refusal would hide it.

• The list is complete from the first letter: what is capped is how many annotations are offered, not how many names are looked
at, so @S reaches SuppressWarnings past the hundreds of classes also starting with S.

• Accepting one adds its import, and the ones you accept come first for as long as the project stays open — never written to disk, never above an
import the file already made.

title: Abbreviations
text:
Type psf and the list offers public static final, with psfi and psfs under it for
int and String. These are IntelliJ's own Java abbreviations, deliberately — fifteen years of psf should work
here without configuring anything.

Family — Abbreviations

Modifiers — pf, prf, psf, psfi,psfs, prsf, prsfi, prsfs, psvm for a main

Printing — sout, souf, serr

Statements — fori, ifn, inn, thr, iter

• Several blanks are walked with Tab, and the body is re-indented to where it lands — a psvm three levels
into a class arrives lined up.

• They are added to what the index found, never substituted: a field called psfCount still appears, under them.

• Offered only where a bare word is typed — after a . the list answers "what members does this have".

• Abbreviations of your own sit beside them, written as code templates — see Code templates.
Yours are not Java's: the language in a template's name says where it is offered, so a dbg.rs.jinja
expands in a Rust file, answered by rust-analyzer, and one written with no language expands in any file. The
built-in family above stays Java's.

iter is the one that reads the surrounding code: it loops over the nearest array or Iterable local or parameter
in scope, with the element type and a name spelled the project's way (var from Java 10). It is offered only where such a variable
exists, at the start of a statement, and its row says which variable it loops over.

Abbreviations that would have to guess — a version that guesses writes a name that is not there. iter is offered only when
there is something to iterate.

title: Postfix templates
text:
Write the expression first, then say what to do with it:

`, 'java')}

The point is not keystrokes: it lets you think in the order you think — the value, then the control flow around it — instead of committing to an
if ( before you know what goes in it. They appear in the completion list under the name you type, with IntelliJ's names on purpose.

What a template writes depends on the type of the expression, and a template is only listed where it applies:
.for on a collection or an array, .if on a boolean, .nn on a value that can be null,
.ifpe on an Optional. The names it proposes come from the code, spelled in the project's naming convention for local variables or, where none is set, in the one the
file's names follow — orders.for declares an order
of the element type — and the imports its text needs are added with it. Templates appear once the type is known and you have started typing a name
after the dot.

Family — Templates

Null checks — .nn / .notnull, .null, .reqnonnull

Conditions — .if, .else, .while, .not, .assert, .switch

Loops — .for / .iter, .fori, .forr, .forEach, .stream

Optional — .opt, .optof, .ifp, .ifpe, .ifget, .orThrow, .orGet

Statements — .var, .return, .throw, .try, .twr, .synchronized, .sout, .soutv, .souf, .serr

Expressions — .inst / .instanceof, .cast, .castvar, .par, .arg, .lambda, .format, .new on a class name

They follow the Java level of the file's module, and write what that level compiles rather than disappearing:

Template — Below — From

.var, .for, .twr — the declared type, Order order — Java 10: var order

.inst — instanceof and a cast into a local — Java 16: a type pattern

.ifpe — if (…isPresent()) … else … — Java 9: ifPresentOrElse

.stream on an Optional — map(Stream::of).orElseGet(Stream::empty) — Java 9: not listed, stream() is its member

An expression that does work is never written twice: where the older form needs the value in two places, repo.findById(id).ifget
declares a local for it first, and .fori, whose bound runs on every iteration, is not offered on a call. Templates with no equivalent
at the level — Optional before Java 8, .twr before 7 — are not listed. Rust gets its own postfix set from rust-analyzer, in
the same list.

Postfix templates of your own sit beside them — a template of the Postfix kind, offered on the values it says it applies to. See
Code templates.

title: After a dot
text:
The list is the members of the value on the left, and its postfix templates — nothing else: no keywords, no words from the file, no local names. When
the value's type cannot be worked out, the popup says there are no suggestions rather than offering what cannot follow a dot.

title: Method references
text:
After Type:: or value:: the list is the methods a reference can name, and new for a class that can be
instantiated. The ones that fit the function expected there come first — in optional.map(ResolvedIdentity::|), the instance methods with
no parameters and the static methods taking a ResolvedIdentity — and accepting one writes only the name.

title: Functions passed as arguments
text:
Inside a call that takes a function, the type the function receives is offered first: in identity_resolver.resolve_identity().map(|) it
is ResolvedIdentity, the value inside the Optional. Ctrl+Space with nothing typed opens on it,
preselected, with its import.

title: A declaration's name
text:
After the type of a declaration — a field after its modifiers, a local variable, a method or constructor parameter, a for or
try resource — the name IntelliJ would suggest is drawn ahead of the caret, and Tab writes it:

Written — Suggested

private final OrderRepository — orderRepository

List<Order> , Order[] — orders

Optional<Order> — order

Class<?> — clazz

The name is spelled the project's way: with the convention its naming rules set for fields, local variables or parameters, and where they set none,
with the one the file's names already follow — among identity_resolver fields, private final FilterConfigurator suggests
filter_configurator.

A name already declared where Java would refuse a second one gets a digit (order1). Once you start typing the name, the suggestion stays
only while it continues what you typed. It never appears after return, new or an operator, inside arguments, strings or
comments, or in a class header.

title: Members that do not exist yet
text:
Two families, one gesture: you are in a class body, you start typing a name, and the thing you mean has not been written.

The method this class calls and does not declare:

You wrote randomico() inside a method; now rand in the class body offers to declare it. The call site is the
specification: the arguments' types and names become the signature, what the result is used as becomes the return type, and a call from a
static method asks for a static one — the reading the Create method quick fix makes, so the popup and
Alt+Enter cannot describe one member two ways.

• It is read from the tree, not from the diagnostic — which is what survives typing. A half-written name in a class body is a syntax
error, and while it lasts its member is not validated, so the red mark under randomico() disappears exactly when the offer is wanted.
The call is still in the tree.

• It reads the calls made on this class from elsewhere in the file, which a nested class needs:
c.randomico("ciao") written in the outer class, on an instance of the inner one, makes ra in the inner class offer it — as
public, since another class calls it. Only a receiver whose type resolves to the class you are in counts.

• A method reference asks as surely as a call: after .map(this::toIdentity), toId in the class body offers
toIdentity with the signature of the functional interface it is passed as — and draws it as ghost text when it is the only
match.

• A method the class inherits is not missing: the supertypes are walked first, and an unreadable hierarchy means silence.

title: The accessors a field is missing
text:
Typing getCust in a class body offers getCustomer(), and accepting writes the whole method:

`, 'java')}

• getXor isX for a primitive boolean — what JavaBeans says and what reflecting frameworks look for

• setXwith this. on the assignment: the parameter shadows the field

• withXthe builder-style setter, assigning and returning the object so calls chain — the member Generate writes under "With"

A final field is offered a getter and nothing else; a static one no withX, with no this to return.
A field named isActive keeps its prefix and is set and chained by its property: setActive, withActive.

As ghost text
When exactly one candidate matches, the answer also appears ahead of the caret — → public String getCustomer() { … } — written with Tab. Two candidates produce nothing, however close the second: ghost text reads like text already there, so being wrong costs trust.
In the open popup
The grey text previews the highlighted row, following the arrows — on one line, since the popup opens right under the caret. It is the popup's selection drawn, not a second proposal: Tab still belongs to the popup.
With the popup closed
After Esc, or with the auto-popup off, the proposal is drawn in full, and Tab writes it.

Only at a member position — not in a method body, where getCustomer is a call, and not after a dot; only for a field
with no accessor already; and never on an empty prefix. Generate (Alt+Insert) is still the
place for the whole set, with the style options — fluent accessors, snake_case names, final parameters. A completion takes the
conventional form.

title: Ghost text for certain continuations
text:
Beside the accessors above, two more continuations are drawn ahead of the caret, because each can only be one thing. Tab writes it;
anything else you type replaces it, and when there is any doubt nothing is drawn. Settings → Completion → Ghost text for certain
continuations turns both off.

A caught exception's name
catch (IOException draws e, spelled the project's way, and e1 when e is already in scope —
a catch parameter may not shadow a local. Qualified types, final and a multi-catch are read; nothing is drawn once a name is started.
The next case
On an empty line after the last arm of a switch over an enum, the first constant not yet covered, in declaration order, written in the
style of the arms already there (case X: or case X ->). Not drawn when there is a default, a pattern or
null label, an arm that falls through, or a selector whose enum cannot be read.

title: Generated members
text:
Plenty of Java members exist at compile time and nowhere in the source. Bennu models them, so completion, hover, find usages and the checks treat
them like any declaration.

From the language

Records

An accessor per component — p.x(), not getX() — the backing fields, the canonical constructor, and toString, equals, hashCode. A member the record writes itself always wins.

When the file imports Lombok

Lombok

@Getter, @Setter, @Data, @Value accessors, @With copies, the @Slf4j log, the @AllArgsConstructor and @RequiredArgsConstructor constructors — on an enum with valued constants too — and @UtilityClass, making every member static and the class final.

That is what makes the annotation mean anything — your own @Data in another package generates nothing. A record's members need no such gate.

@Accessors
At class or field level, the field's winning: fluent = true names both accessors after the field — o.customer() reads, o.customer("x") writes — and chain = true, which fluent turns on by itself, makes the setter return the object. The prefix element is not read yet.
AccessLevel
On @Getter and @Setter, at class or field level: @Setter(AccessLevel.PACKAGE) is a package-private setter; AccessLevel.NONE generates nothing. Generated constructors carry their access the same way, with the parameters Lombok gives them — @RequiredArgsConstructor takes the unassigned final fields and the @NonNull ones.
@Builder
The class it really generates: the static builder(), a setter per field returning the builder, build(), and with toBuilder = true the instance toBuilder(). @Singular adds the single-element adder — .tag("a"), named from the field or @Singular("tag") — and clearTags(). A @Builder.Default field is still a constructor parameter. On a constructor or a static factory, the builder takes that element's parameters, is named after what it builds, and build() returns that.
@Value, @FieldDefaults
@Value makes the fields private final and the class final, though the source writes none of it. @FieldDefaults(makeFinal = true, level = …) does the same, with @NonFinal and @PackagePrivate honoured.
@Delegate, @SuperBuilder
Their members depend on a type that cannot be read while indexing, so the type is marked as having more members than the list — nothing concludes "no such method" from their absence, and the rest of it is checked as before.

A primitive boolean field already starting with is keeps it, as Lombok does:

Field — Getter — Setter

boolean isRunning — isRunning() — setRunning(…)

boolean is_attivo — is_attivo() — —

boolean isattivo — isIsattivo() — what follows is is lowercase — —

Boolean active — getActive() — a wrapper is a plain getter — —

There is no name in the source to jump to, so it has nothing to open. Go-to on the backing field, or a record's component, works.

title: Frames, values & watches
text: Build, run & test

title: Frames, values & watches
text: Where the debugger puts what it found, and how to read a value that is bigger than the row it sits in.

title: It all happens in the Run console
text:
There is no separate Debug window: debugging is the same launch with more to look at, so Run (Alt+R) grows what the moment needs. While a
session is attached, the transport controls sit on the left of the status row. While the program is stopped, two columns open left of the transcript:

What got here

Frames

Library and JDK frames are muted and open their source or a decompiled stub. A run of consecutive library frames folds into one row — a stop inside a framework is forty frames around your three; ⊟ turns folding off.

In the selected frame

Variables and watches

The frame's variables, with your watches underneath — both read again when you pick another frame.

• The editor follows the debugger. Every stop and step opens the current frame's file at its line — stepping into a method changes the tab for you — and the stopped line
is banded full width with a bar down its left edge.

• Both columns are resizable, and each collapses to a labelled strip from the ⇤ in its header, giving the transcript the rest. Where you left them is remembered.

• When the program stops, Bennu comes to the front and opens the console: a breakpoint fires because of something in another window, and the editor is where the answer
is. A step does not raise it — you did that here.

title: Stepping
text:
Key — Does

F8 — Step over

F7 — Step into

Shift+F8 — Step out

F9 — Resume

A step passes straight through the JDK, Spring's AOP machinery, Reactor and the logging façades, rather than stopping in ArrayList.add or walking
ReflectiveMethodInvocation.proceed a dozen times. Landing in a proxy — a Spring CGLIB or Hibernate stand-in, methods existing only at runtime — it keeps going,
so stepping into service.place(order) arrives at place.

Which packages are passed through is a judgement about whose code you are debugging: Settings → Java → Debugger lists them, and removing org.springframework.* steps
into Spring. A pattern may carry * at one end only — the VM refuses anything else, and one bad entry would stop stepping altogether — so it is checked as you type. Changes apply
to the next launch.

title: Reading a value whole
text:
The variables tree fetches a row's contents only when opened — a stopped program is a graph, and walking it eagerly would be a round trip per node nobody looked at. That is wrong for one job:
a struct of fifteen fields, four of them structs, is nineteen disclosure triangles before you can read it, and then no longer fits on screen.

So every row with something inside carries a {'{}'} button — on hover and on keyboard focus — reading the value and everything under it at once, as text you can scroll, search
with the editor's find, and copy. The tree is for looking around; this is for looking at. It works on a watch row too.

RON
The value is a Rust value, and RON keeps the three distinctions JSON throws away: a struct is not a map, a tuple (1, "x") is not a list, a variant is a name. It is RON-shaped, as the footer says — a debugger reports names, rendered values and children, not a type system — for reading, not parsing.
Literals stay literals
A value the debugger already rendered as a literal is printed, not opened. Rust's formatters render a String, PathBuf or OsString as text and offer children — a byte buffer underneath — and following those turns a path into four levels of internals and a row per character. A size=3 describes a container, so it still opens.
Bounded, and saying so
Each value is a round trip against a suspended program, so the walk stops at a depth, a node count, a container width or a time budget — and says so, at the top and where it stopped. A value containing itself is named as a cycle. The same modal works on a Java object graph.

title: Watches
text:
A watch is a path: order, order.customer.name, items[2]. On a native session it takes a leading * to follow a reference —
*head — and *self.next means what the same line means in the source, the star binding looser than the dots.

A path is read out of the variables tree, not handed to an evaluator. So v[0] in the watch box and [0] under v are the same row, mean the
same whichever adapter resolved, and know which variant an enum actually holds — which no static type can. A subscript is fetched alone, so v[400000] on a million-element
Vec is a fair question with an exact answer. Watches are saved with the breakpoints.

Anything not a path goes to the debugger's own evaluator, and Bennu says which and what it can do:

CodeLLDB prefix — Evaluator

/se — the default — Its own reader: follows the formatters, runs nothing in the program

/nat — LLDB's own parser

/py — Python, with $name from the frame

The other two adapters have one evaluator, so a prefix they lack is refused by name rather than sent back as a syntax error about a slash.

Not a debugger limitation: a debugger can only call a function that is in the binary, and a generic function nobody called was never compiled. So v.len(), a macro, a
turbofish, ?, .await and a closure each come back with one line saying why, and what to read instead.

title: Things worth knowing
text:
Objects show fields, not toString()
An object reads Order@1f3c and expands to its real fields, superclasses included. toString() would read better and would run application code in a paused program — blocking on a lock the stopped thread holds, changing state, or throwing.
Variable names need -g
Maven compiles with full debug information by default. A class compiled without it still holds breakpoints — the line table is separate — but the panel shows only this.
The launch is not frozen
The program starts and runs, so a start-up breakpoint may pass before the debugger listens. Tick Suspend the VM until the debugger has attached in the configuration, and every debug launch begins stopped, waiting for Resume.
Detach is not Stop
Detaching leaves the program running without a debugger; the console's ■ ends it. A suspended VM holds its locks and port, so a session left paused looks exactly like a hang — the rail's Debug dot turns amber to say so.

title: Debugging
text: Build, run & test

title: Debugging
text: Stop the program where you want it and read what it is actually holding — Java over JDWP, Rust through a debug adapter, with the same panel and the same gestures for both.

title: Starting
text:
Gesture — Does

Shift+F9, or 🐞 beside ▶ — Launches the active configuration with a debugger attached

A click in the left margin, outside the line numbers — Sets or clears a breakpoint

Ctrl+F8 — Sets or clears one on the caret's line

Ctrl+Shift+F8 — The breakpoint list

Breakpoints belong to the project, not to a session: they are kept in .arbor/bennu/config.toml beside the run configurations, still there tomorrow, and a
launch installs whatever is set. What happens once the program stops — frames, values, watches — is Frames, values & watches.

More than one at once:

Several programs can be under the debugger together, each in its own console tab. A session and its tab are one thing, so the panel shows the one whose tab is in front, and moving
along the strip moves the frames, variables and watches with it. What the VM made of each breakpoint is per session — two VMs on one project can disagree, one having loaded the class.
